At the technical heart of Wiles's argument lies the modularity lifting theorem, which converts a global assertion—that an elliptic curve E is modular, meaning its entire compatible family of ℓ-adic Galois representations arises from a weight-two newform—into a residual hypothesis that can be checked at a single prime. The theorem states, in essence, that if E is semistable over **Q** and the mod p representation ρ̄(E,p): Gal(**Q**̄/**Q**) → GL₂(**F**_p), obtained by reducing ρ(E,p) modulo p, is irreducible and modular, then *every* p-adic lift of ρ̄(E,p) of the appropriate local type is modular, and in particular E itself is modular. Wiles established this via deformation theory: one fixes ramification conditions and studies the universal deformation ring R, which parametrizes all p-adic lifts of ρ̄(E,p) satisfying those conditions, alongside the Hecke algebra **T**, which parametrizes precisely the modular lifts. There is a natural surjection R → **T**, and the goal becomes proving it is an isomorphism—an "R = **T**" theorem. Wiles first treated the *minimal* case, using Galois cohomology to bound the tangent space of R by a Selmer group and a numerical criterion involving complete intersections to force equality; the Taylor–Wiles patching method, devised after a gap was found in the 1993 manuscript, supplied the auxiliary primes needed to verify the criterion, and an inductive level-raising argument then extended the result to arbitrary ramification.

The dichotomy between reducible and irreducible cases hinges on whether ρ̄(E,p) preserves a one-dimensional subspace—equivalently, whether E admits a rational p-isogeny. Irreducibility is an essential hypothesis of the deformation machinery, so Wiles required a separate means of establishing modularity of the residual representation itself. The choice p = 3 is decisive here, because GL₂(**F**₃) is a solvable group, its projective image being the symmetric group S₄. The Langlands–Tunnell theorem, proved using cyclic base change and the Arthur–Selberg trace formula, shows that any odd irreducible two-dimensional Galois representation with solvable image is modular; consequently, whenever ρ̄(E,3) is irreducible, its modularity is *automatic*. The lifting theorem then immediately yields the modularity of every semistable curve whose mod 3 representation is irreducible, disposing of the generic case in one stroke.

The reducible case at p = 3—curves admitting a rational 3-isogeny—demands the ingenious "3–5 switch." Semistability prevents ρ̄(E,5) from also being reducible, so Wiles works instead with p = 5. Because the modular curve X(5) has genus zero, its rational points are plentiful, and one can produce a second semistable curve E′ with ρ̄(E′,5) ≅ ρ̄(E,5) but with ρ̄(E′,3) irreducible. Langlands–Tunnell applies to E′ at p = 3, making E′ modular; since ρ̄(E,5) is isomorphic to the modular representation ρ̄(E′,5), it too is modular, and the lifting theorem at p = 5 then delivers the modularity of E. Every semistable elliptic curve over **Q** is therefore modular—contradicting Ribet's theorem that the Frey curve is not, and completing the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem.

**Unconcealing the Real: Technology as a Mode of Truth in Heidegger**

For Heidegger, the question concerning technology cannot be answered by the familiar instrumental definition—technology as a means devised for human ends—because that definition, while correct, never touches the essence of technology. Tracing instrumentality back through the Aristotelian doctrine of the four causes, Heidegger argues that causality itself is a mode of bringing-forth (*Her-vor-bringen*), of occasioning something to pass from concealment into unconcealment. Such bringing-forth is what the Greeks named *poiēsis*: it occurs in *physis*, where beings arise of themselves, as the blossom bursts into bloom, and in *technē*, where the artisan brings forth the chalice or the craftsman reveals the work. *Technē* thus originally signifies not mechanical fabrication but a knowing that discloses; it belongs to *poiēsis*, and in Greek antiquity it embraced both handicraft and the fine arts. What is brought forth comes out of hiddenness into presence, and this event of disclosure is precisely what the Greeks called *alētheia*—truth as unconcealment (*Unverborgenheit*), prior to any correctness of propositions. On this ground Heidegger can assert that technology "is a mode of revealing," that it comes to presence "in the realm where revealing and unconcealment take place, where *alētheia*, truth, happens." The essence of technology and the essence of truth are internally linked: to build, to produce, to craft is already to let reality appear in a determinate way.

Modern technology, however, is a revealing of a decisively different kind: it does not bring forth, it challenges-forth (*herausfordern*), setting upon nature so that nature is ordered to deliver energy that can be extracted, transformed, stored, and redistributed. The hydroelectric plant set into the Rhine challenges the river to yield electrical power, unlike the old wooden bridge that merely joins bank to bank; the windmill turns in the wind without stockpiling its force. What is disclosed through this challenging appears as standing-reserve (*Bestand*)—no longer even an object standing over against us, but an orderable inventory on call for further ordering. The gathering of this revealing that orders the real as standing-reserve Heidegger names Enframing (*Ge-stell*), the essence of modern technology, which is itself nothing technological. Critically, Enframing remains a mode of *alētheia*: it genuinely discloses the real, yet it does so in a manner that simultaneously conceals the thingness of things and occludes every other possible mode of revealing. Where everything is ordered as standing-reserve, unconcealment itself withdraws, and truth as disclosure is eclipsed by truth as the calculable ordering of objects—a destiny in which humanity itself threatens to be reduced to standing-reserve.

This double character of revealing explains Heidegger's vocabulary of destining (*Geschick*). Because man does not invent the manner in which the real discloses itself but is "started upon the way" of a revealing, revealing is a "sending-that-gathers" (*versammeltes Schicken*), a destining "from out of which the essence of all history [*Geschichte*] is determined." History is therefore "neither simply the object of written chronicle nor simply the fulfillment of human activity"; human activity first becomes history as something destined, and "only the destining into objectifying representation" renders the historical accessible as an object of historiographical science. The same logic governs the destiny of truth itself: the Greek experience of *alētheia* was progressively recast as Roman *veritas* and then as correctness and certainty, such that our common-sense notion of truth as the correspondence of representation to object is a late offspring of the destining into objectification. Technology is consequently a "human way" of revealing only in a qualified sense: humanity does not control the revealing, yet humanity is needed by it, as the one who keeps watch over unconcealment. Recognizing technology as a destining of truth opens what Heidegger calls the "free relationship" to it—the recollection, with Hölderlin, that where the danger of total ordering grows, the saving power of a renewed openness to *alētheia* grows as well.

## Prenatal Brain Differentiation and the Hardwiring Debate

The decoupling of neural and genital sexual differentiation is mechanistically plausible because the two processes are governed by different molecular cascades operating in different critical windows. External genitalia masculinize early in the first trimester (roughly weeks 7–12 of human gestation), driven primarily by dihydrotestosterone (DHT), which is produced locally when 5α-reductase converts testosterone in genital skin. The brain, by contrast, differentiates later and expresses a distinct enzymatic and receptor landscape: hypothalamic and limbic regions such as the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BSTc) and the interstitial nuclei of the anterior hypothalamus (INAH3) express aromatase, androgen receptors, and estrogen receptors in region- and stage-specific patterns. In rodents, brain masculinization depends largely on aromatization of testosterone to estradiol within neurons, whereas in primates direct androgen receptor signaling appears more important; either way, the brain's "masculinizing signal" is chemically different from the genital one. Consequently, any factor that alters one pathway but not the other—variation in aromatase or 5α-reductase activity, fluctuating fetal or maternal hormone levels during a particular gestational window, placental metabolism, maternal stress–mediated glucocorticoid exposure, or endocrine-disrupting compounds—could shift genital and neural development in discordant directions. Direct genetic effects add another layer: work with the "four core genotypes" mouse model (Arnold and colleagues) shows that XX versus XY chromosome complement influences neural and behavioral phenotypes independently of gonadal hormones, and SRY itself is expressed in the brain. Finally, prenatal steroids leave durable epigenetic marks—sex-specific DNA methylation and histone modifications in the preoptic area and related nuclei (e.g., Nugent et al., 2015)—that constitute a molecular memory capable of channeling later maturation along divergent trajectories even when circulating hormone levels converge after birth.

(1995) reported that the BSTc, which is normally larger and contains more somatostatin neurons in men, was female-sized in male-to-female transgender individuals; Kruijver et al. (2000) replicated this with neuron counts and showed the pattern held in subjects who had never received cross-sex hormones, arguing against an artifact of adult treatment. Garcia-Falgueras and Swaab (2008) similarly reported female-typical INAH3 volume and neuron number in trans women. These findings converge with complementary evidence: girls with congenital adrenal hyperplasia, exposed prenatally to elevated androgens, show masculinized play behavior and modestly elevated rates of gender dysphoria; many individuals with 5α-reductase deficiency raised as girls adopt male identities at puberty; and twin studies indicate substantially higher concordance for transgender identity among monozygotic than dizygotic pairs (Heylens et al., 2012), implying heritable, plausibly prenatal, contributions. Yet significant caveats temper strong conclusions. The BSTc and INAH3 studies rest on very small samples of postmortem tissue with potential confounds (illness, medication, cause of death); crucially, Chung, De Vries, and Swaab (2002) found that BSTc dimorphism itself does not emerge until around puberty, meaning the structure is not visibly "sexed" at birth; and the data are correlational—no study demonstrates that a given nucleus *causes* identity rather than merely correlating with it, and group means overlap enough that these structures cannot classify any individual's identity.

Does this demonstrate that gender identity is "hardwired" prenatally? The weight of current evidence supports a more cautious formulation: prenatal hormonal and genetic mechanisms appear to *bias* rather than *determine* identity. ## The Script

The lines you provided are the opening verses of Molière's *Les Femmes savantes* (1672). The script below vectorizes each line as a TF‑IDF-weighted bag of character n‑grams, computes the full pairwise cosine-similarity matrix, and reports the argmax (nearest neighbor) for every line.

```python
"""
Nearest-neighbor retrieval for a small corpus of French verse lines,
using character n-gram TF-IDF vectors and cosine similarity.
"""

import math
import unicodedata
from collections import Counter

import numpy as np
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

CORPUS = [
    "D'où me vient ce désordre, Aufide, et que veut dire",
    "Madame, il était temps qu'il vous vînt du secours:",
    "Ah! Monsieur, c'est donc vous?",
    "Ami, j'ai beau rêver, toute ma rêverie",
    "Ne me parle plus tant de joie et d'hyménéé;",
    "Il est vrai, Cléobule, et je veux l'avouer",
    "Laisse-moi mon chagrin, tout injuste qu'il est;",
    "Ton frère, je l'avoue, a beacoup de mérite",
    "J'en demeure d'accord, chacun a sa méthode;",
    "Pour prix de votre amour que vous peignez extrême,",
]


def normalize(text: str) -> str:
    """Lowercase and canonicalize Unicode so accented characters compare consistently."""
    return unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text.lower())


def main() -> None:
    normalized = [normalize(line) for line in CORPUS]

    # 1. VECTORIZE: character n-grams (2-4) within word boundaries, TF-IDF weighted.
    vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer(analyzer="char_wb", ngram_range=(2, 4),
                                 sublinear_tf=True)
    X = vectorizer.fit_transform(normalized)   # sparse matrix, shape (10, n_features)

    # 2. SIMILARITY: S[i, j] = cos(x_i, x_j) for every ordered pair of lines.
    S = cosine_similarity(X)

    # 3. NEAREST NEIGHBOR: mask the diagonal (self-similarity = 1) and take argmax.
    np.fill_diagonal(S, -np.inf)
    neighbors = np.argmax(S, axis=1)

    # 4. REPORT.
    for i, j in enumerate(neighbors):
        print(f"[{i}] {CORPUS[i]}")
        print(f"     └─ nearest: [{j}] {CORPUS[j]}  (cosine = {S[i, j]:.4f})\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

def char_ngrams(text, ns=(2, 3, 4)):
    padded = f" {text} "                       # boundary markers, as in 'char_wb'
    return Counter(g for n in ns
                   for i in range(len(padded) - n + 1)
                   for g in [padded[i:i + n]])

docs = [char_ngrams(normalize(t)) for t in CORPUS]
N = len(docs)

df = Counter(g for d in docs for g in d)                     # document frequency
idf = {g: math.log((1 + N) / (1 + c)) + 1 for g, c in df.items()}

vecs = [{g: (1 + math.log(tf)) * idf[g] for g, tf in d.items()} for d in docs]

def cosine(a, b):
    dot = sum(w * b.get(g, 0.0) for g, w in a.items())
    return dot / (math.sqrt(sum(w * w for w in a.values())) *
                  math.sqrt(sum(w * w for w in b.values())))

for i, a in enumerate(vecs):
    sims = [(cosine(a, b), j) for j, b in enumerate(vecs) if j != i]
    best, j = max(sims)
    print(f"[{i}] nearest = [{j}]  cosine = {best:.4f}")
```

## `babel.sh` — A Deterministic Generator for the Library of Babel

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# babel.sh — deterministic generator for Borges' Library of Babel
#
# Canon: 25 symbols (22 letters a-v, space, period, comma);
#        80 chars/line, 40 lines/page  -> 3,200 chars/page;
#        410 pages/book                -> 1,312,000 chars/book.
#
# Indexing: a book index N (0 <= N < 25^1312000) is read as a 1,312,000-digit
# base-25 number; each digit selects one symbol from the alphabet. The mapping
# is a bijection, so EVERY index yields a valid book and EVERY book has an index.
#
# Usage:
#   ./babel.sh <book_index> [page]   # print page (0..409) of book <book_index>
#   ./babel.sh --page <page_index>   # print page by direct index (0..25^3200-1)
#   ./babel.sh --encode "text ..."   # inverse map: text -> its page index
#   ./babel.sh --stats               # print the combinatorial constants
#
set -euo pipefail

exec python3 - "$@" <<'PYEOF'
import sys

ALPHABET   = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuv .,"   # 22 letters + space + '.' + ',' = 25
BASE       = len(ALPHABET)                 # 25
WIDTH      = 80                            # characters per line
LINES      = 40                            # lines per page
PAGE_CHARS = LINES * WIDTH                 # 3,200
BOOK_PAGES = 410                           # pages per book
BOOK_CHARS = BOOK_PAGES * PAGE_CHARS       # 1,312,000

def digits_to_page(chunk: int) -> str:
    """Render the least-significant 3,200 base-25 digits of chunk as a page."""
    out = []
    for _ in range(PAGE_CHARS):
        chunk, d = divmod(chunk, BASE)     # d = next base-25 digit
        out.append(ALPHABET[d])
    out.reverse()                          # digits came out least-significant first
    return "\n".join("".join(out[i:i+WIDTH]) for i in range(0, PAGE_CHARS, WIDTH))

def page_of_book(book: int, page: int) -> str:
    if not 0 <= book < pow(BASE, BOOK_CHARS):
        sys.exit("error: book index outside [0, 25^1312000)")
    if not 0 <= page < BOOK_PAGES:
        sys.exit("error: page outside [0, 409]")
    shift = pow(BASE, page * PAGE_CHARS)   # 25^(3200*page): skip earlier pages
    chunk = (book // shift) % pow(BASE, PAGE_CHARS)
    return digits_to_page(chunk)

def page_by_index(idx: int) -> str:
    if not 0 <= idx < pow(BASE, PAGE_CHARS):
        sys.exit("error: page index outside [0, 25^3200)")
    return digits_to_page(idx)

def encode_page(text: str) -> int:
    """Inverse bijection: map a text (<=3200 chars) to its page index."""
    pos = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(ALPHABET)}
    text = text.lower()[:PAGE_CHARS].ljust(PAGE_CHARS, "a")   # pad with digit 0
    n = 0
    for c in text:
        if c not in pos:
            sys.exit(f"error: character {c!r} not in the 25-symbol alphabet")
        n = n * BASE + pos[c]              # Horner's method, most-significant first
    return n

argv = sys.argv[1:]
if not argv:
    sys.exit("usage: babel.sh <book> [page] | --page <idx> | --encode <text> | --stats")

if argv[0] == "--stats":
    total = pow(BASE, BOOK_CHARS)
    print(f"alphabet size      : {BASE}")
    print(f"chars per book     : {BOOK_CHARS:,}")
    print(f"total books        : 25^1,312,000 = {len(str(total)):,} decimal digits")
    print(f"total single pages : 25^3,200 = {len(str(pow(BASE, PAGE_CHARS))):,} decimal digits")
elif argv[0] == "--page":
    print(page_by_index(int(argv[1])))
elif argv[0] == "--encode":
    print(encode_page(" ".join(argv[1:])))
else:
    book

"""
lorenz_rk4_sensitivity.py

Solve the Lorenz system with a classical 4th-order Runge-Kutta (RK4)
integrator and demonstrate sensitive dependence on initial conditions.

System:
    dx/dt = sigma * (y - x)
    dy/dt = x * (rho - z) - y
    dz/dt = x*y - beta*z

Standard chaotic parameters: sigma = 10, beta = 8/3, rho = 28.
Two trajectories are started 1e-4 apart in x; their Euclidean separation
is tracked over time, and a finite-time estimate of the largest Lyapunov
exponent is extracted from the exponential-growth regime.

Requires: NumPy (matplotlib and SciPy optional, used only for extras).
"""

import numpy as np


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Vector field
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def lorenz(state, sigma, beta, rho):
    """Right-hand side of the Lorenz system, f(state) = d(state)/dt."""
    x, y, z = state
    return np.array([
        sigma * (y - x),        # dx/dt
        x * (rho - z) - y,      # dy/dt
        x * y - beta * z,       # dz/dt
    ])


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Classical 4th-order Runge-Kutta
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def rk4_step(f, state, dt, *args):
    """Advance the autonomous system one step of size dt."""
    k1 = f(state, *args)
    k2 = f(state + 0.5 * dt * k1, *args)
    k3 = f(state + 0.5 * dt * k2, *args)
    k4 = f(state + dt * k3, *args)
    return state + (dt / 6.0) * (k1 + 2.0 * k2 + 2.0 * k3 + k4)


def integrate(f, state0, times, *args):
    """Integrate from state0 over the uniform time grid; return trajectory."""
    n = times.size
    dt = times[1] - times[0]
    traj = np.empty((n, state0.size))
    traj[0] = state0
    s = state0.copy()
    for i in range(n - 1):
        s = rk4_step(f, s, dt, *args)
        traj[i + 1] = s
    return traj


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Main experiment
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def main():
    sigma, beta, rho = 10.0, 8.0 / 3.0, 28.0

    dt    = 0.001                      # RK4 step size
    t_max = 40.0
    times = np.arange(0.0, t_max + dt, dt)

    # Infinitesimally different initial conditions
    state_A0 = np.array([1.0,    1.0, 1.0])
    state_B0 = np.array([1.0001, 1.0, 1.0])   # perturbed by 1e-4 in x

    traj_A = integrate(lorenz, state_A0, times, sigma, beta, rho)
    traj_B = integrate(lorenz, state_B0, times, sigma, beta, rho)

    # Euclidean separation |x_A(t) - x_B(t)|
    distance = np.linalg.norm(traj_A - traj_B, axis=1)
    d0 = distance[0]

    # Decorrelation time: first crossing of an O(1) threshold
    threshold = 1.0
    hits = np.nonzero(distance >= threshold)[0]
    t_decor = times[hits[0]] if hits.size else float("nan")

    # Finite-time largest Lyapunov exponent: slope of log d(t) in the
    # linear (exponential-growth) window, before saturation sets in.
    mask = (distance > 10.0 * d0) & (distance < 0.1)
    lam_est = np.polyfit(times[mask], np.log(distance[mask]), 1)[0] \
        if np.count_nonzero(mask) > 10 else float("nan")

    print(f"RK4 steps             : {times.size - 1}  (dt = {dt})")
    print(f"Initial separation    : {d0:.3e}")
    print(f"Separation at t={t_max:.0f}   : {distance[-1]:.3e}")
    print(f"Decorrelation time    : t = {t_decor:.2f}  (separation >= {threshold})")

"""
range_sum_benchmark.py

Comparative benchmark of two strategies for dynamic range-sum queries:
  1. NaiveRangeSum : O(1) point update, O(N) range query
  2. SegmentTree   : O(log N) point update, O(log N) range query (built from scratch)

Synthetic workload: N = 100,000 elements, Q = 50,000 intermixed operations.
"""

import random
import time


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Strategy 1: Naive contiguous array
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
class NaiveRangeSum:
    """Stores raw values. Updates are O(1); each range query re-scans
    the whole interval and therefore costs O(N) worst case."""

    def __init__(self, data):
        self.a = list(data)

    def update(self, idx, value):
        self.a[idx] = value

    def query(self, left, right):              # inclusive [left, right]
        return sum(self.a[left:right + 1])


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Strategy 2: Segment Tree (from scratch, array-based, no libraries)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
class SegmentTree:
    """Complete binary tree stored implicitly in a flat array of size 2*P,
    where P is the smallest power of two >= N.  Node i's children are 2i and
    2i+1; leaves live at indices [P, P+N).  Every internal node caches the
    sum of the segment it covers."""

    def __init__(self, data):
        n = len(data)
        p = 1
        while p < n:                       # round up to a power of two
            p <<= 1
        self.P = p
        self.tree = [0] * (2 * p)
        self.tree[p:p + n] = data          # lay down the leaves ...
        for i in range(p - 1, 0, -1):      # ... then build parents bottom-up
            self.tree[i] = self.tree[2 * i] + self.tree[2 * i + 1]

    def update(self, idx, value):
        i = idx + self.P
        self.tree[i] = value
        i >>= 1
        while i >= 1:                      # repair the root-to-leaf path
            self.tree[i] = self.tree[2 * i] + self.tree[2 * i + 1]
            i >>= 1

    def query(self, left, right):          # inclusive [left, right]
        left += self.P
        right += self.P
        total = 0
        while left <= right:
            if left & 1:                   # left is a right child -> take it
                total += self.tree[left]
                left += 1
            if not (right & 1):            # right is a left child -> take it
                total += self.tree[right]
                right -= 1
            left >>= 1
            right >>= 1
        return total
